title: The voice in the desert (Matthew 3:1–12)
hookLine: John the Baptist in camel hair, eating locusts, calling people to turn around
last: MOST OF HIS LIFE WAS ORDINARY.

lines: A MAN SHOUTING IN THE DESERT.
cards: Out past the towns, in the dry country near the Jordan River, a man is shouting. He wears a rough garment of camel's hair with a leather belt. He eats locusts and wild honey.

No house, no title, no invitation. And people come, Matthew says, from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan. They stand in the river, confess their sins, and he baptizes them.
This is John, the one Christians call the Baptist, a relative of Jesus. His message fits in one breath.

teach.h: DO PENANCE: THE KINGDOM IS AT HAND.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims Bible, the old Catholic English translation: "Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." The King James says repent. Both reach for one Greek word, metanoia.
Meta, after or beyond. Noia, from the word for mind.
A change of mind, a turning around. Not feeling bad, first of all: a new direction.
The Douay-Rheims followed the Latin Bible's do penance, and that wording is one reason Catholics speak of the sacrament of penance: confession carries an echo of this call.
Matthew hears John in the prophet Isaiah, centuries earlier: "A voice of one crying in the desert, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths."
Isaiah pictures a road made ready for a king: low places filled, hills brought down, the crooked made straight.

teach.h: A KING IS COMING. FIX THE ROAD.
teach.b: John's message: a king is coming, and the road is you. He isn't gentle about it. When religious leaders come to watch, he tells them to bring forth fruit worthy of penance, to show the turning in how they live.
The axe, he says, is already at the root of the trees.
But he points away from himself.

teach.h: PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.
teach.b: Someone mightier is coming after him, and John isn't worthy even to carry his sandals. The Church keeps John close.
His voice fills the Sundays of Advent, and both his birth, on June twenty-fourth, and his death have their own feasts.

how: Catholics hear John the Baptist's call in the Advent Sunday readings and answer it in the sacrament of penance (confession), where a person names their sins, receives absolution and is given a penance.

o: a calm, still mind beyond all thought
feeling deep shame for what you did
a change of mind, a turning around

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a change of mind, a turning

s: "do penance" and "repent" translate the same Greek word
both render metanoia, a change of mind. the Douay-Rheims follows the Latin, the King James the Greek.
John the Baptist and John the apostle are the same person
two different Johns. the Baptist prepared the way; the apostle was one of the twelve.
John says he is the one everyone is waiting for
he points away from himself: someone mightier is coming, whose sandals he isn't worthy to carry.

games.q: you're John. religious leaders come out to the river to see what you're doing. what do you say?
o: welcome them warmly and baptize them first.
tell them to show their turning by how they live.
send them away without a word.
games.why: he challenges them: bring forth fruit worthy of penance. the turning has to show up in a life, not only at a riverbank.

practice: Settle, and let one thing come to mind that you'd like to turn from: a habit that keeps the road crooked, a sharp way of talking, a grudge you keep feeding. Name it plainly, inside, without trying to fix it yet.
If you pray, hold it up to God and ask for help turning; if you don't, just sit with the naming.

wordCard.voice: Metanoia. Greek for a change of mind, a turning around: John's call at the Jordan.

orig.note: Greek: a change of mind, a turning around. The Latin Bible rendered John's call as do penance.

carryVoice: Your line: make straight the way. The road John meant runs through a life. Thirty-one days in.
